Visible-light mediated cascade cyclization of
ene-vinylidenecyclopropanes: access to
ﬂuorinated heterocyclic compounds†
Zhe Meng,a Xiaoyu Zhanga and Min Shi
 *a,b
A ﬂuoroalkylation and cycloisomerization cascade reaction of ene-VDCP with ethyl iododi ﬂuoroacetate
or perﬂuoroalkyl iodide upon visible-light irradiation is disclosed in this paper, a ﬀording the desired ﬂuori-
nated cyclization products in moderate to good yields under mild reaction conditions along with good
functional group tolerance. Mechanistic investigations were also performed with a light on/o ﬀ experi-
ment, ﬂuorescence quenching experiment and quantum yield measurement, suggesting that a radical
chain process exists in this process.
Fluorinated heterocyclic compounds are important building
blocks, which widely exist in bioactive molecules and natural
products.1 In addition, they are also core structural motifs in
many synthesized organic compounds or pharmaceuticals. In
fact, 30% of all agrochemicals approximately and 20% of phar-
maceuticals currently on the market contain fluorine atoms.
1g
In general, introducing fluoroalkyl groups on heterocyclic
stents can significantly enhance the pharmacokinetic pro-
perties of drugs by improving absorption, distribution, hydro-
phobicity and metabolism. 2 Therefore, it is very important to
develop novel and e ﬃcient synthesis methods for heterocyclic
compounds incorporating fluorine or fluorinated moieties.
Thus, research on the synthesis methods of such compounds
has always been a hot topic, attracting attention from organic
chemists.
3
In recent years, intramolecular tandem cyclization initiated
by photocatalytic free radicals has been extensively reported.
Through photoredox catalysis methods, simple alkenes can be
utilized as feedstock materials to undergo the addition of
fluoroalkyl radicals, generating fluorinated compounds via
trifluoromethylation, iodinated perfluoroalkylation, thiodi-
fluoroalkylation, and cyanofluoroalkylation (Scheme 1, a).
4 On
the other hand, the addition of fluoroalkyl radicals generated
from a fluoroalkane or other fluorinated precursors upon
photoredox catalysis into alkenes can a ﬀord alkyl radicals,
which can subsequently react with other intramolecular unsa-
turated functional groups, such as alkyne,
5 cyan,6 aldehyde,7
imine8 and aromatic groups in an intramolecular manner, 9,10
to form fluorinated heterocyclic compounds (Scheme 1, b).
However, only a few methods have been developed for the syn-
thesis of fluorinated heterocyclic compounds through a
tandem cyclization reaction under visible light irradiation thus
far. For example, Wang ’s group
5a reported a visible light-
mediated bicyclization process employing ethyl bromofluoro-
acetate and 1,7-enyne for the synthesis of polycyclic compounds
containing fluoroalkyl groups and heteroatoms. Moreover,

Zhang’s group 6 developed a visible-light-induced free radical
cascade cyclization reaction of 2-isocyanoaryl sulfide with ethyl
bromodifluoroacetate for the construction of 2-CF 2/CF3-substi-
tuted benzothiazoles. At the present stage, the development of
novel and atom/step economical tandem cyclization reactions
for the rapid construction of fluorinated heterocylic products
is highly desirable.
Although previous reports already demonstrated a wide
range of unsaturated groups in olefinic substrates, the exploi-
tation of new olefinic substrates is still desired. We attempted
to introduce olefinic groups into vinylidenecyclopropanes
(VDCPs)
11,12 that have been continuously studied by our
research group, and hypothesized that ene-vinylidenecyclopro-
panes could be excellent candidates for exploiting new
methods for fluoroalkylation and cyclization due to their mul-
tiple reaction sites. Herein, we wish to report a novel synthesis
method for preparing fluorinated heterocyclic compounds
through the generation of a fluoroalkyl radical upon photo-
redox catalysis by visible light irradiation and coupling with
ene-VDCPs for a tandem ring opening/iodofluoroalkylation/
cycloisomerization process (Scheme 1, c). The successful devel-
opment of this new synthesis strategy can also enrich the
chemistry of VDCPs.
Considering that homolytic cleavage of iodofluoroalkanes
can be directly achieved by visible light irradiation, we initiated
our investigation from the reaction between ene-VDCP 1a and
ethyl iododifluoroacetate under an argon atmosphere with
blue LED irradiation at room temperature. After screening the
solvent, lamp wattage and reaction time without adding a
photocatalyst, we found that the desired product 2a can be
formed in 80% NMR yield (see Table S1 in the ESI †); however,
the reaction always gave a complex mixture, from which it is
diﬃcult to get the pure product 2a. Next, we tried adding a
photocatalyst to the reaction system and conducting the reac-
tion with 0.5 mol% fac-Ir( ppy)
3 as the photocatalyst and using
dioxane as the solvent at room temperature upon irradiation
with a 30 W blue LED for 12 h. We identified that the desired
product 2a could be isolated in 83% yield in pure form.
Other photocatalysts such as Ir[dF(CF
3)( ppy)]2[dCF3(bpy)]PF6,
Ir[dF(CF3)( ppy)]2(dtbbpy)PF6, Ir( ppy) 2(dtbbpy)PF6 and
Ir(dFCF3ppy)2(bpy)PF6 turned out to be less e ﬃcient (Table 1,
entries 2 – 5). The screening of solvents revealed that dioxane
was more suitable than others (Table 1, entries 6 – 8).
Ethyl bromodifluoroacetate could also be used as the Rf
radical precursor to react with 2a,a ﬀording the desired
product in 65% yield. However, when bromoperfluorohexane
was utilized as the Rf radical precursor to react with 2a,n o
reaction occurred (Table 1, entries 9 and 10). Control experi-
ments demonstrated that no product 2a was detected in the
absence of visible light or under an ambient atmosphere
(Table 1, entries 11 and 12).
With the optimized reaction conditions in hand, the gener-
ality of the production of fluorinated heterocyclic compounds
2 was explored using a series of substituted ene-vinylidene-
cyclopropanes as substrates and the results are shown in
Scheme 2. With ene-VDCPs 1a–g as the substrates (R
1 =H ,R 2 =
alkyl group), the desired products 2a–g were obtained in 57% –
83% yields as a single diastereoisomer and an increase of the
steric hindrance of the alkyl group gradually decreased the
yield of 2. For ene-VDCPs 1h–j, in which an aromatic ring (R
1 =
Ar) was introduced, the desired products 2h–j were obtained in
73– 85% yields regardless of whether they are electron-neutral,
-donating or -withdrawing aromatic rings. As for ene-VDCP 1k,
the corresponding product 2k was formed in 50% yield pre-
sumably due to the steric e ﬀect of the cyclohexyl group. It is
worth mentioning that the use of 1-butenyl group substituted
ene-VDCP 1l as the substrate a ﬀorded the desired product 2l
with a yield of 54%, indicating that the reaction has excellent
functional group tolerance. In the case of substrate 1m,i n
which the carbon chain of the olefinic moiety has been
extended for another one carbon atom, the six-membered ring
product 2m was obtained in 43% yield. Obviously, compared
with N-Ts-protected ene-VCDPs, N-Bs-protected substrates 1n–
p also performed very well, a ﬀording the desired products 2n–
p in 40 – 76% yields. Using ene-VDCP 1q or 1r connected by an
O atom or a C atom as a substrate did not give the desired
product 2q or 2r under the standard conditions. We speculate
that when ene-VDCP was connected with an NTs moiety, the
olefin and VDCP units were close to each other due to the
Thorpe– Ingold e ﬀect in space, making the reaction proceed
smoothly. However, when ene-VDCP was connected with a
carbon or oxygen atom, the olefin and VDCP units could not
be so close in space, ensuring that no reaction could take
place or the reaction is di ﬃcult to occur, giving the desired
product in low yield. The structure of 2k was determined by
X-ray crystallographic analysis and its ORTEP drawing is
shown in Scheme 2.

In order to further demonstrate the generality of this syn-
thesis strategy, we then turned our attention to the scope of
perfluoroalkyl iodides (Scheme 3). Similarly, using ene-VDCPs
1 as the substrates, the desired cyclic perfluoroalkylated pro-
ducts 3a–g were obtained in moderate to good yields. Using
methyl group-substituted VDCPs 1 (R1 =H ,R 2 = Me) as sub-
strates gave the corresponding products 3a–b in 65 – 70%
yields.
Introducing aromatic substituents in VDCPs 1 (R1 = Ar)
gave the desired products 3c–e in 82– 93% yields. Further inves-
tigation indicated that the reaction also tolerated cyclohexyl
and 1-butenyl groups (R 2 group), giving the corresponding pro-
ducts 3f and 3g in 48% and 45% yields, respectively. When
ene-VDCP connected by an O atom was used as the substrate
to react with iodoperfluorobutane, the desired product 3h was
obtained in 23% yield.
To gain more insights into the reaction mechanism,
we conducted several control experiments (Fig. 1 and
Schemes 4 and 5). 13 First, when the radical scavenger 2,2,6,6-
tetramethyl-1-piperidinyloxy (TEMPO) (2.0 equiv.) was added
to the reaction system, the reaction was completely inhibited

under the standard conditions and the corresponding TEMPO-
incorporated perfluoroalkyl radical was isolated in 20% yield
(Scheme 4). Fluorescence quenching analysis revealed that
ICF
2CO2Et was an e ﬀective quencher for the excited-state
photocatalyst (Fig. 1). Next, to clarify whether the reaction also
proceeded through a radical chain process, 14 we performed
light on/oﬀ experiments with 1h as a substrate, disclosing that
the reaction also proceeded when the light was turned o ﬀ
(Scheme 5). Furthermore, the quantum yield was measured as
Φ = 23 in this reaction, making the intervention of the radical
chain mechanism likely (see the ESI † for details).
On the basis of the mechanistic investigations discussed
above as well as the related previous reports,
15 a plausible reac-
tion mechanism was proposed, as shown in Scheme 6.
Irradiation of fac-IrIII( ppy)3 with blue light generates the
excited-state of fac-IrIII*( ppy)3, which undergoes oxidative
quenching with ethyl iododifluoroacetate through a SET
process to give an electrophilic fluoroalkyl radical, tending to
react with the electron-rich alkene moiety VDCP 1 to furnish a
radical intermediate A. Then, intramolecular cycloaddition
takes place to a ﬀord radical intermediate B, which undergoes
a cyclopropane ring-opening reaction to give alkynyl radical
intermediate C. There are two pathways to obtain the desired
product 2. Path I is a radical chain process, where the radical
C reacts with ethyl iododifluoroacetate to a ﬀord product 2 with
the regeneration of the fluoroalkyl radical. Another pathway,
path II, involves the oxidation of radical C by Ir
IV to aﬀord cat-
ionic intermediate D, which subsequently undergoes nucleo-
philic addition of an iodide anion also to generate the final
product 2.
In summary, we have developed a novel protocol for visible-
light-mediated carbocyclization reactions of ene-VDCPs with
ethyl iododifluoroacetate and perfluoroalkane for the synthesis
of fluorinated heterocyclic compounds under mild conditions.
The reaction had good functional group tolerance and sub-
strate scope, a ﬀording the desired products in moderate to
good yields. These five or six-membered fluorine-containing
heterocyclic compounds may be useful as potential intermedi-
ates in organic synthesis and medicinal chemistry. The
mechanistic study indicated that the reaction involved a free
radical chain process and a sequential fluoroalkylation and
cycloisomerization process. Further investigations on expand-
ing the reaction of this synthesis method are ongoing in our
laboratory.

Visible-light mediated cascade cyclization of
ene-vinylidenecyclopropanes: access to
ﬂuorinated heterocyclic compounds†
Zhe Meng,a Xiaoyu Zhanga and Min Shi
 *a,b
A ﬂuoroalkylation and cycloisomerization cascade reaction of ene-VDCP with ethyl iododi ﬂuoroacetate
or perﬂuoroalkyl iodide upon visible-light irradiation is disclosed in this paper, a ﬀording the desired ﬂuori-
nated cyclization products in moderate to good yields under mild reaction conditions along with good
functional group tolerance. Mechanistic investigations were also performed with a light on/o ﬀ experi-
ment, ﬂuorescence quenching experiment and quantum yield measurement, suggesting that a radical
chain process exists in this process.
Fluorinated heterocyclic compounds are important building
blocks, which widely exist in bioactive molecules and natural
products.1 In addition, they are also core structural motifs in
many synthesized organic compounds or pharmaceuticals. In
fact, 30% of all agrochemicals approximately and 20% of phar-
maceuticals currently on the market contain fluorine atoms.
1g
In general, introducing fluoroalkyl groups on heterocyclic
stents can significantly enhance the pharmacokinetic pro-
perties of drugs by improving absorption, distribution, hydro-
phobicity and metabolism. 2 Therefore, it is very important to
develop novel and e ﬃcient synthesis methods for heterocyclic
compounds incorporating fluorine or fluorinated moieties.
Thus, research on the synthesis methods of such compounds
has always been a hot topic, attracting attention from organic
chemists.
3
In recent years, intramolecular tandem cyclization initiated
by photocatalytic free radicals has been extensively reported.
Through photoredox catalysis methods, simple alkenes can be
utilized as feedstock materials to undergo the addition of
fluoroalkyl radicals, generating fluorinated compounds via
trifluoromethylation, iodinated perfluoroalkylation, thiodi-
fluoroalkylation, and cyanofluoroalkylation (Scheme 1, a).
4 On
the other hand, the addition of fluoroalkyl radicals generated
from a fluoroalkane or other fluorinated precursors upon
photoredox catalysis into alkenes can a ﬀord alkyl radicals,
which can subsequently react with other intramolecular unsa-
turated functional groups, such as alkyne,
5 cyan,6 aldehyde,7
imine8 and aromatic groups in an intramolecular manner, 9,10
to form fluorinated heterocyclic compounds (Scheme 1, b).
However, only a few methods have been developed for the syn-
thesis of fluorinated heterocyclic compounds through a
tandem cyclization reaction under visible light irradiation thus
far. For example, Wang ’s group
5a reported a visible light-
mediated bicyclization process employing ethyl bromofluoro-
acetate and 1,7-enyne for the synthesis of polycyclic compounds
containing fluoroalkyl groups and heteroatoms. Moreover,

Zhang’s group 6 developed a visible-light-induced free radical
cascade cyclization reaction of 2-isocyanoaryl sulfide with ethyl
bromodifluoroacetate for the construction of 2-CF 2/CF3-substi-
tuted benzothiazoles. At the present stage, the development of
novel and atom/step economical tandem cyclization reactions
for the rapid construction of fluorinated heterocylic products
is highly desirable.
Although previous reports already demonstrated a wide
range of unsaturated groups in olefinic substrates, the exploi-
tation of new olefinic substrates is still desired. We attempted
to introduce olefinic groups into vinylidenecyclopropanes
(VDCPs)
11,12 that have been continuously studied by our
research group, and hypothesized that ene-vinylidenecyclopro-
panes could be excellent candidates for exploiting new
methods for fluoroalkylation and cyclization due to their mul-
tiple reaction sites. Herein, we wish to report a novel synthesis
method for preparing fluorinated heterocyclic compounds
through the generation of a fluoroalkyl radical upon photo-
redox catalysis by visible light irradiation and coupling with
ene-VDCPs for a tandem ring opening/iodofluoroalkylation/
cycloisomerization process (Scheme 1, c). The successful devel-
opment of this new synthesis strategy can also enrich the
chemistry of VDCPs.
Considering that homolytic cleavage of iodofluoroalkanes
can be directly achieved by visible light irradiation, we initiated
our investigation from the reaction between ene-VDCP 1a and
ethyl iododifluoroacetate under an argon atmosphere with
blue LED irradiation at room temperature. After screening the
solvent, lamp wattage and reaction time without adding a
photocatalyst, we found that the desired product 2a can be
formed in 80% NMR yield (see Table S1 in the ESI †); however,
the reaction always gave a complex mixture, from which it is
diﬃcult to get the pure product 2a. Next, we tried adding a
photocatalyst to the reaction system and conducting the reac-
tion with 0.5 mol% fac-Ir( ppy)
3 as the photocatalyst and using
dioxane as the solvent at room temperature upon irradiation
with a 30 W blue LED for 12 h. We identified that the desired
product 2a could be isolated in 83% yield in pure form.
Other photocatalysts such as Ir[dF(CF
3)( ppy)]2[dCF3(bpy)]PF6,
Ir[dF(CF3)( ppy)]2(dtbbpy)PF6, Ir( ppy) 2(dtbbpy)PF6 and
Ir(dFCF3ppy)2(bpy)PF6 turned out to be less e ﬃcient (Table 1,
entries 2 – 5). The screening of solvents revealed that dioxane
was more suitable than others (Table 1, entries 6 – 8).
Ethyl bromodifluoroacetate could also be used as the Rf
radical precursor to react with 2a,a ﬀording the desired
product in 65% yield. However, when bromoperfluorohexane
was utilized as the Rf radical precursor to react with 2a,n o
reaction occurred (Table 1, entries 9 and 10). Control experi-
ments demonstrated that no product 2a was detected in the
absence of visible light or under an ambient atmosphere
(Table 1, entries 11 and 12).
With the optimized reaction conditions in hand, the gener-
ality of the production of fluorinated heterocyclic compounds
2 was explored using a series of substituted ene-vinylidene-
cyclopropanes as substrates and the results are shown in
Scheme 2. With ene-VDCPs 1a–g as the substrates (R
1 =H ,R 2 =
alkyl group), the desired products 2a–g were obtained in 57% –
83% yields as a single diastereoisomer and an increase of the
steric hindrance of the alkyl group gradually decreased the
yield of 2. For ene-VDCPs 1h–j, in which an aromatic ring (R
1 =
Ar) was introduced, the desired products 2h–j were obtained in
73– 85% yields regardless of whether they are electron-neutral,
-donating or -withdrawing aromatic rings. As for ene-VDCP 1k,
the corresponding product 2k was formed in 50% yield pre-
sumably due to the steric e ﬀect of the cyclohexyl group. It is
worth mentioning that the use of 1-butenyl group substituted
ene-VDCP 1l as the substrate a ﬀorded the desired product 2l
with a yield of 54%, indicating that the reaction has excellent
functional group tolerance. In the case of substrate 1m,i n
which the carbon chain of the olefinic moiety has been
extended for another one carbon atom, the six-membered ring
product 2m was obtained in 43% yield. Obviously, compared
with N-Ts-protected ene-VCDPs, N-Bs-protected substrates 1n–
p also performed very well, a ﬀording the desired products 2n–
p in 40 – 76% yields. Using ene-VDCP 1q or 1r connected by an
O atom or a C atom as a substrate did not give the desired
product 2q or 2r under the standard conditions. We speculate
that when ene-VDCP was connected with an NTs moiety, the
olefin and VDCP units were close to each other due to the
Thorpe– Ingold e ﬀect in space, making the reaction proceed
smoothly. However, when ene-VDCP was connected with a
carbon or oxygen atom, the olefin and VDCP units could not
be so close in space, ensuring that no reaction could take
place or the reaction is di ﬃcult to occur, giving the desired
product in low yield. The structure of 2k was determined by
X-ray crystallographic analysis and its ORTEP drawing is
shown in Scheme 2.

In order to further demonstrate the generality of this syn-
thesis strategy, we then turned our attention to the scope of
perfluoroalkyl iodides (Scheme 3). Similarly, using ene-VDCPs
1 as the substrates, the desired cyclic perfluoroalkylated pro-
ducts 3a–g were obtained in moderate to good yields. Using
methyl group-substituted VDCPs 1 (R1 =H ,R 2 = Me) as sub-
strates gave the corresponding products 3a–b in 65 – 70%
yields.
Introducing aromatic substituents in VDCPs 1 (R1 = Ar)
gave the desired products 3c–e in 82– 93% yields. Further inves-
tigation indicated that the reaction also tolerated cyclohexyl
and 1-butenyl groups (R 2 group), giving the corresponding pro-
ducts 3f and 3g in 48% and 45% yields, respectively. When
ene-VDCP connected by an O atom was used as the substrate
to react with iodoperfluorobutane, the desired product 3h was
obtained in 23% yield.
To gain more insights into the reaction mechanism,
we conducted several control experiments (Fig. 1 and
Schemes 4 and 5). 13 First, when the radical scavenger 2,2,6,6-
tetramethyl-1-piperidinyloxy (TEMPO) (2.0 equiv.) was added
to the reaction system, the reaction was completely inhibited

under the standard conditions and the corresponding TEMPO-
incorporated perfluoroalkyl radical was isolated in 20% yield
(Scheme 4). Fluorescence quenching analysis revealed that
ICF
2CO2Et was an e ﬀective quencher for the excited-state
photocatalyst (Fig. 1). Next, to clarify whether the reaction also
proceeded through a radical chain process, 14 we performed
light on/oﬀ experiments with 1h as a substrate, disclosing that
the reaction also proceeded when the light was turned o ﬀ
(Scheme 5). Furthermore, the quantum yield was measured as
Φ = 23 in this reaction, making the intervention of the radical
chain mechanism likely (see the ESI † for details).
On the basis of the mechanistic investigations discussed
above as well as the related previous reports,
15 a plausible reac-
tion mechanism was proposed, as shown in Scheme 6.
Irradiation of fac-IrIII( ppy)3 with blue light generates the
excited-state of fac-IrIII*( ppy)3, which undergoes oxidative
quenching with ethyl iododifluoroacetate through a SET
process to give an electrophilic fluoroalkyl radical, tending to
react with the electron-rich alkene moiety VDCP 1 to furnish a
radical intermediate A. Then, intramolecular cycloaddition
takes place to a ﬀord radical intermediate B, which undergoes
a cyclopropane ring-opening reaction to give alkynyl radical
intermediate C. There are two pathways to obtain the desired
product 2. Path I is a radical chain process, where the radical
C reacts with ethyl iododifluoroacetate to a ﬀord product 2 with
the regeneration of the fluoroalkyl radical. Another pathway,
path II, involves the oxidation of radical C by Ir
IV to aﬀord cat-
ionic intermediate D, which subsequently undergoes nucleo-
philic addition of an iodide anion also to generate the final
product 2.
In summary, we have developed a novel protocol for visible-
light-mediated carbocyclization reactions of ene-VDCPs with
ethyl iododifluoroacetate and perfluoroalkane for the synthesis
of fluorinated heterocyclic compounds under mild conditions.
The reaction had good functional group tolerance and sub-
strate scope, a ﬀording the desired products in moderate to
good yields. These five or six-membered fluorine-containing
heterocyclic compounds may be useful as potential intermedi-
ates in organic synthesis and medicinal chemistry. The
mechanistic study indicated that the reaction involved a free
radical chain process and a sequential fluoroalkylation and
cycloisomerization process. Further investigations on expand-
ing the reaction of this synthesis method are ongoing in our
laboratory.
